q: The Swarajists' strategy of entering the legislative councils is best described as an approach to:
o: 'End or mend' the councils — using them as an arena to expose weaknesses or obstruct government business
Boycott elections entirely while criticising the councils from outside
Fully cooperate with the government in administering the councils
Seek dominion status through negotiations within the councils

q: According to the Swarajist Manifesto (October 1923), if their demand for self-government within councils was rejected, they would adopt a policy of:
o: Immediate resignation from all council seats
Complete silence and non-participation in council debates
Uniform, continuous and consistent obstruction within the councils to make governance impossible
Armed uprising against the government

q: Gandhi, initially opposed to council entry, gradually reconciled with the Swarajists after his release from prison in February 1924, and their agreement was formally endorsed at which Congress session, the only one Gandhi ever presided over?
o: Belgaum session (December 1924)
Karachi session (1931)
Lahore session (1929)
Gaya session (1922)

q: The Swarajist Party lost significant Muslim support chiefly because:
o: The party failed to support the tenants' (mostly Muslim) cause against zamindars in Bengal
It refused to contest any elections in Muslim-majority areas
It supported the Simon Commission's recommendations
It banned Muslims from party membership

q: Which Swarajist leader was elected speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly in 1925, considered a notable achievement of the party?
o: Motilal Nehru
Vithalbhai Patel
N.C. Kelkar
C.R. Das

q: Which of the following is identified as a drawback of the Swarajist strategy?
o: They lacked a policy to coordinate their council-based militancy with mass struggle outside, relying mainly on newspaper reporting
They completely avoided using obstructionist tactics
They refused to ever contest any elections
They had no support from coalition partners at any point

q: A key criticism of the 'constructive work' programme, as noted in the chapter, was that:
o: National education mainly benefited the urban lower middle classes and rich peasants, while khadi remained costlier than imported cloth for the poor
It received unanimous support from all Congress leaders without dissent
It had no impact whatsoever on any social group
It was fully successful in eliminating untouchability's economic roots

q: The Kanpur Bolshevik Conspiracy Case of 1924, in which several communists including S.A. Dange, Muzaffar Ahmed, Shaukat Usmani and Nalini Gupta were jailed, was followed by which 1925 event that formalised the CPI's foundation within India?
o: The Belgaum Congress session
The formation of the AITUC
The Indian Communist Conference at Kanpur
The Meerut Conspiracy Case

q: The two main strands of revolutionary activity with a socialist turn during the 1920s operated respectively in:
o: Madras and Bombay
Only in Bengal, with no activity elsewhere
Punjab-UP-Bihar (Hindustan Republican Association) and Bengal (Yugantar/Anushilan groups, later Chittagong Revolt Group)
Only in Punjab, with no activity in Bengal

q: The Hindustan Republican Association (HRA), founded in October 1924 at Kanpur by Ramprasad Bismil, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee and Sachin Sanyal, aimed to establish which form of government?
o: A Federal Republic of the United States of India based on adult franchise
A dominion within the British Commonwealth
A theocratic state based on religious law
A constitutional monarchy under an Indian prince

q: The Kakori Robbery (August 1925), the HRA's most significant action, involved:
o: Looting official railway cash from the 8-Down train near Kakori village, close to Lucknow
A bomb thrown in the Central Legislative Assembly
An armoury raid in Chittagong
An assassination attempt on the Calcutta Police Commissioner

q: The HRA was reorganised as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) at a historic meeting in September 1928 at:
o: Chittagong, Bengal
Lahore, Punjab
The ruins of Ferozshah Kotla, Delhi
Kakori village, near Lucknow

q: The assassination of the police official Saunders in Lahore (December 1928) by Bhagat Singh, Azad and Rajguru was in retaliation for:
o: The Kakori Robbery arrests
The Jallianwala Bagh Massacre
The Meerut Conspiracy Case trials
The lathi-charge injuries that led to the death of Lala Lajpat Rai during an anti-Simon Commission protest

q: Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly on April 8, 1929, to protest against:
o: The Government of India Act, 1919
The Public Safety Bill and the Trade Disputes Bill, aimed at curtailing civil liberties
The partition of Bengal
The Rowlatt Act

q: The book 'The Philosophy of the Bomb', articulating the revolutionary position of the HSRA, was written by:
o: Bhagat Singh
Ramprasad Bismil
Sachin Sanyal
Bhagwaticharan Vohra

q: Which of the following rules, drafted by Bhagat Singh for the Punjab Naujawan Bharat Sabha, reflected his secular outlook?
o: Members were required to take religious oaths before joining
Members must belong to a single religious community for organisational unity
Members would have nothing to do with communal bodies and would propagate tolerance, treating religion as a matter of personal belief
Members would prioritise religious education over political work

q: Bhagat Singh's redefinition of revolution, as expressed in his court statement, held that revolution meant:
o: The restoration of pre-colonial monarchical structures
Purely individual acts of violence against colonial officials
Changing the present unjust order of things, not merely 'the cult of bomb and pistol' or personal vendetta
A religious crusade against foreign rule

q: Bhagat Singh's class analysis held that peasants needed liberation from which combination of oppressive forces?
o: Only capitalists, regardless of nationality
Only indigenous landlords, with no reference to colonial rule
Only the foreign colonial yoke
Both the foreign colonial yoke and the yoke of landlords and capitalists

q: In Bengal, after C.R. Das's death (1925), the Bengal Congress split into two factions led by:
o: Surya Sen and Jatin Das
J.M. Sengupta (backed by the Anushilan group) and Subhash Bose (backed by the Yugantar group)
Motilal Nehru and Vallabhbhai Patel
Bhagat Singh and Chandra Shekhar Azad

q: The Chittagong Armoury Raid, organised by Surya Sen and associates including Anant Singh and Ganesh Ghosh, took place in:
o: April 1930

q: Surya Sen was arrested in February 1933 and executed in:
o: January 1934

q: Santi Ghosh and Suniti Chandheri, school girls of Comilla, are notable for:
o: Founding the Punjab Naujawan Bharat Sabha
Shooting dead the district magistrate in December 1931
Leading the Chittagong Armoury Raid
Organising the Kakori Robbery

q: Which of the following was a noteworthy feature of the new phase of Bengal's revolutionary movement under Surya Sen, distinguishing it from the earlier Anushilan/Yugantar phase?
o: Complete exclusion of women from all revolutionary work
An increased emphasis on individual assassination over group action
A total rejection of any connection with the Indian National Congress
A shedding of earlier Hindu religious rituals, which facilitated the participation of Muslims in the movement

q: In 1933, Jawaharlal Nehru was arrested for sedition and sentenced to two years primarily because he had:
o: Assassinated a British official
Led the Meerut Conspiracy Case defendants
Organised the Chittagong Armoury Raid
Condemned imperialism and praised the heroism of the revolutionaries
